pr_body:
Bazel aims to support arbitrary file system path encodings (even raw byte sequences) by attempting to force the JVM to use a Latin-1 locale for OS interactions. As a result, Bazel internally encodes `String`s as raw byte arrays with a Latin-1 coder and no encoding information. Whenever it interacts with encoding-aware APIs, this may require a reencoding of the `String` contents, depending on the OS and availability of a Latin-1 locale.

This PR introduces the concepts of *internal*, *Unicode*, and *platform* strings and adds dedicated optimized functions for converting between these three types (see the class comment on the new `StringEncoding` helper class for details). These functions are then used to standardize and fix conversion throughout the code base. As a result, a number of new end-to-end integration tests for the handling of Unicode in file paths, command-line arguments and environment variables now pass. 

Full support for Unicode beyond the current active code page on Windows is left to a follow-up PR as it may require patching the embedded JDK.

* Replace ad-hoc conversion logic with the new consistent set of helper functions.
* Make more parts of the Bazel client's Windows implementation Unicode-aware. This also fixes the behavior of `SetEnv` on Windows, which previously would remove an environment variable if passed an empty value for it, which doesn't match the Unix behavior.
* Drop the `charset` parameter from all methods related to parameter files. The `ISO-8859-1` vs. `UTF-8` choice was flawed since Bazel's internal string representation doesn't maintain any encoding information - `ISO-8859-1` just meant "write out raw bytes", which is the only choice that matches what arguments would look like if passed on the command line.
* Convert server args to the internal string representation. The arguments for requests to the server were already converted to Bazel's internal string representation, which resulted in a mismatch between `--client_cwd` and `--workspace_directory` if the workspace path contains non-ASCII characters.
* Read the downloader config using Bazel's filesystem implementation.
* Make `MacOSXFsEventsDiffAwareness` UTF-8 aware. It previously used the `GetStringUTF` JNI method, which, despite its name, doesn't return the UTF-8 representation of a string, but modified CESU-8 (nobody ever wants this).
* Correctly reencode path strings for `LocalDiffAwareness`.
* Correctly reencode the value of `user.dir`.
* Correctly turn `ExecRequest` fields into strings for `ProcessBuilder` for `bazel --batch run`. This makes it possible to reenable the `test_consistent_command_line_encoding` test, fixing #1775.
* Fix encoding issues in `TargetCompleteEvents`.
* Fix encoding issues in `SubprocessFactory` implementations.
* Drop obsolete warning if `file.encoding` doesn't equal `ISO-8859-1` as file names are encoded with `sun.jnu.encoding` now.
* Consistently reencode internal strings passed into and out of `FileSystem` implementations, e.g. if reading a symlink target. Tests are added that verify the interaction between `FileSystem` implementations and the Java (N)IO APIs on Unicode file paths.

Fixes #1775 
Fixes #11602
Fixes #18293 
Work towards #374
Work towards #23859

There are two, mostly equally valid ways to make things right: one can either do what you are doing in this change and commit to the "bytes as Latin-1" approach or dispense with it, use UTF-8 everywhere and not support files with badly encoded names in the future.

I did some archaeology and if this bug I found from 2008 February (not a typo) is any indication, the reason why the "bytes as Latin-1" approach was taken is indeed file names with bad encoding. I suspect that now that UTF-8 is way more prevalent, that's much less of a problem today. 

I don't have a strong opinion (currently, this might change the more I think about it) about which way Bazel should go other than that "bytes as Latin-1" is definitely the odd choice. Have you considered this approach?

> I don't have a strong opinion (currently, this might change the more I think about it) about which way Bazel should go other than that "bytes as Latin-1" is definitely the odd choice. Have you considered this approach?

Yes, and I think that we should ultimately switch to it to reduce the complexity of the code. But I think that getting "bytes as Latin-1" done right is the safer path to that goal as it allows us to introduce meaningful end-to-end tests in a mostly backwards compatible way. Once we are at that point, we can reason about what use cases we would break if we transitioned to the "everything UTF-8" approach. If we do that right away, we may end up breaking users in unforeseen ways.

Roughly half of the changes in this PR are needed for both approaches anyway. If we want to fully migrate to UTF-8 later, we essentially only need to start using the new encoding functions in `UnixFileSystem`, inline them to no-ops in all other places and consume files as UTF-8 rather than Latin-1. I would be happy to help with this and suggest changes, but this is ultimately something a Googler would be better positioned to do, simply because of the internal-only Linux distributions being used at Google that I have no knowledge of (and that, for example, don't yet have a `C.UTF-8` locale).

I did a bout of debugging to see how to fix the newly added tests, and I still don't know :(

I looked at `UnixDigestHashAttributeNameTest.testGetNioPath_externalUtf8[SHA-256]`.

I do know how it breaks, though: our Google-internal test framework cleverly unsets `LANG`, which means that `sun.jnu.encoding` will be `ANSI_X3.4-1968`, which is basically ASCII. Then `StringEncoding.internalToPlatform()` will do reencoding, and recover the original string with the basil/Japanese characters. Then, `sun.nio.fs.UnixPath.encode()` correctly determines that that cannot be represented if the platform encoding is ASCII and thus dies.

There are two issues:
1. Bazel hard-wires ISO8859-1 as LANG in its server binary, but our internal test battery uses an unset `LANG`, therefore we are testing things in a way that's not consistent with production. 
2. The test does not actually work with ISO8859-1 as `sun.jnu.encoding` because then it runs into the same "unmappable character" issue

The obvious solution would be to temporarily set `sun.jnu.encoding` in that test, but that doesn't seem to be possible: it doesn't look like the JVM honors `-Dsun.jnu.encoding` on the command line, setting it using `System.setProperty()` doesn't work because its value is cached in many places (e.g. `sun.nio.fs.Util.jnuEncoding`) and the `java_test.env=` attribute doesn't work due to the above hard-wiring.

So other than reaching into that class by reflection, I don't see how the test can work other than by assuming that UTF-8 is the encoding it's running under, which is not the case at Google.

> The test does not actually work with ISO8859-1 as sun.jnu.encoding because then it runs into the same "unmappable character" issue

Did you verify this? I think it's not true: If `sun.jnu.encoding` is Latin-1 on Unix, where native filesystem APIs are byte-based, the JVM will behave just like `UnixFileSystem` and read and produce "raw bytes in Latin-1 coder" strings, which is good enough for the test to pass.

> Bazel hard-wires ISO8859-1 as LANG in its server binary, but our internal test battery uses an unset LANG, therefore we are testing things in a way that's not consistent with production.

The Bazel test uses Bazel's Java stub template, which always forces a UTF-8 locale for tests to run in. I don't know what Blaze's Java stub template looks like, but would it work to explicitly set `LANG` or `LC_ALL` via `env`, just like `StringEncodingTest` does?

I thought about this and I think the root cause of the issue is that Bazel does one thing (UTF-8), Blaze does another thing (ISO8859-1) and the tests do a third thing (ASCII). I feel uneasy that the tests replicate the production environment that unfaithfully, but it's not an easy fix because there isn't a way to set `LANG` for Java tests in all scenarios (we unmodifiably unset `LANG` internally regardless of what `java_test.env` says so the trick you suggest doesn't work :(

The tests would still be useful in Bazel's presubmit and it's far easier to provide comprehensive coverage of all file systems via a Java test. I would thus prefer to either wrap them in this way or to disable them for Blaze (e.g. via `assume` on the locale).

issue_context.title: Bazel fails to start if username contains accented characters on Windows
issue_context.body:
### Description of the bug:


All Bazel Windows executables fail during startup if the path to the user's home directory contains accented characters. The accented character in most cases comes from the username. Crashes occur either because Bazel can't create necessary files and folders, or because it can't load certain dynamic libraries because the accent is mishandled in the path. 

Bazelisk is also affected. 

Changing the default code page on Windows to use utf-8 fixes some of the early start-up crashes, but Bazel will eventually mishandle a path and fail. This can be done by going to the system's Language settings, selecting Administrative language settings, clicking Change system locale... and checking the Beta: Use Unicode UTF-8 for worldwide language support box and then restarting the system.

I tested this with the 7.0.0 prerelease build as well. This version also fails. However, some improvements have been made in this version of Bazel. With the code page change described above Bazel will finish launching, however, it still emits an error. See output section at the end of this document 

### What's the simplest, easiest way to reproduce this bug? Please provide a minimal example if possible.


1. Create a new user with an accented character in their username ("István" in my case). 
2. Download the latest version of Bazel (6.1.2 as of writing). 
3. Invoke the downloaded binary. 
4. Bazel will crash during startup. Error message says it wasn't able to create it's directories due to malformed path. 



### Which operating system are you running Bazel on?


Windows 10/11

### What is the output of `bazel info release`?


WARNING: Invoking Bazel in batch mode since it is not invoked from within a workspace (below a directory having a WORKSPACE file). Error occurred during initialization of VM Unable to load native library:

### If `bazel info release` returns `development version` or `(@non-git)`, tell us how you built Bazel.


N/A

### What's the output of `git remote get-url origin; git rev-parse master; git rev-parse HEAD` ?


```text
N/A
```


### Have you found anything relevant by searching the web?

Similar previous issue https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/3821

How are platform strings different from Unicode strings?

AFAIU Java Strings don't have a user-visible "encoding" value so I maybe you mean the encoding of their internal byte array? But that can't be cause you just use `new String()` in `internalToPlatform()` below just like in `internalToUnicode()`.
